title: The alphabet prayer
hook: a man who knows no prayers recites the alphabet and asks God to arrange the letters
tomorrow: the fire, the place, the prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday a shepherd boy blew his whistle on Yom Kippur. Your line was the whistle opened heaven. Did you offer something in your own way? Day two hundred ninety-six.

You want to write a card to someone who's grieving, and nothing sounds right. You start, delete it, start again. Or you want to apologize, and every sentence comes out wrong. Sometimes we have the feeling but not the words. Today's Hasidic story is about a man in exactly that spot, standing before God with a full heart and an empty vocabulary. And the thing he did is so simple it almost sounds like a joke. It isn't. It's one of the most loved stories in the tradition.
screen: `THE CARD YOU CAN'T WRITE.` → `THE FEELING, BUT NOT THE WORDS.` → `A FULL HEART, NO VOCABULARY.`

segments.voice: The story is told in many ways. In one telling, a simple Jew, a farmer or a villager, is stuck somewhere on the way when it's time to pray, and he doesn't have his prayer book. He never learned the prayers by heart. He only knows the letters. So he stands and says the Hebrew alphabet, slowly, one letter after another. Alef. Bet. Gimel. Dalet. All twenty-two. And then he says something like this: Master of the world, I don't know the prayers. But you know them. Here are all the letters. Please, you arrange them into the right words. In the Hasidic telling, a great rebbe hears of it, or sees it in a vision, and says this was the finest prayer offered that day. Why does this land so hard? Because everything anyone ever said to God was made from those same letters. Psalms, blessings, the Shema: all of it is alef-bet, arranged. The man isn't skipping the prayer. He's handing over all of it, raw, and trusting the one who hears to put it together. There's a real line in the daily prayers that has the same humility. Before the central standing prayer, Jews say a verse from the Psalms: "O Lord, open Thou my lips." Even the most learned begin by admitting they need help to find the words.
screen: `NO BOOK, NO PRAYERS, ONLY LETTERS.` · `ALEF, BET, GIMEL, DALET.` · `YOU ARRANGE THEM.` · `O LORD, OPEN THOU MY LIPS.` · then, large: `ARRANGE THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer what you have. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you want to say, to God if you pray, or to someone in your life, and can't find the words for. Don't try to find them now. Instead, just offer the raw pieces. A name. A feeling. A memory. Set them down, one by one, like letters. If you pray, you can ask for them to be arranged. If not, simply trust that what's true in them will come through. The bell holds the time.
The alphabet prayer. A man who knew no prayers said the alphabet, and asked God to arrange the letters into the right words.
Your line: arrange the letters. Today, when you can't find the right words, offer the plain ones you have. Day two hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Before the Amidah, the central standing prayer, Jews quietly say the verse O Lord, open Thou my lips, and many teachers tell the alphabet story to comfort those who don't know the Hebrew prayers.

original.note: Hebrew: alef-bet, the first two letters, and the name for the alphabet.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man who didn't know how to pray.
what it means: every prayer is made of the same letters; he offered them all.
what a scholar hears: the tale has many folk versions; the verse before the Amidah is Psalm 51:17.

notes: Folk tale with many versions; attributions vary (the Baal Shem Tov, Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, others). Presented as 'told in many ways'. No verified early written source.
Psalm 51:17 in JPS 1917 numbering (51:15 in some English Bibles). Check JPS 1917 wording ('O Lord, open Thou my lips').
The man's words to God are described, not written as a new prayer.
